text: A lookup sheet, not a tutorial. Everything here appears in the labs; this page exists so you are not scrolling back through three weeks of notes to remember an argument name.

title: R and Quarto Reference

Getting data in







Task
Code




Load a package
library(readr)


Read a CSV
d <- read_csv("data/file.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)


Check it loaded
nrow(d), dim(d), names(d)

str(d)


First / last rows

section: Getting at parts of a data frame

Getting at parts of a data frame



Task
Code




One column as a vector
d$score or d[["score"]]


Several columns
d[, c("score", "deaths")]


Rows meeting a condition
d[d$score > 1500, ]


Rows and columns at once
d[d$build == "A", c("score", "deaths")]

title: R and Quarto Reference
text:
Describing one variable



Task
Code




Everything at once
summary(x)


Centre
mean(x), median(x)


Spread
sd(x), range(x), IQR(x)


Quartiles
quantile(x)


A specific percentile
quantile(x, 0.99)


Count a category
table(d$cohort)


Cross-tabulate two
table(d$build, d$quit_reason)


Ignore missing values
add na.rm = TRUE

title: R and Quarto Reference
text:
Describing by group







Task
Code




One summary per group
tapply(d$score, d$cohort, median)


Several columns at once
aggregate(score ~ cohort, data = d, FUN = median)

title: R and Quarto Reference
text:
Plots



Task
Code




Distribution of one variable
hist(x, breaks = 20)


Compare groups
boxplot(score ~ cohort, data = d)


Two variables against each other
plot(d$mobility, d$distance_m)


A series over time
plot(x, y, type = "l")


A reference line
abline(h = 16.7, lty = 2)


Counts as bars
barplot(table(d$quit_reason))



Useful arguments for all of them: main = (title), xlab = / ylab = (axis labels), col = (fill colour).

text:
Errors you will meet







Message
What it means




could not find function "..."
Missing library() call, or a typo in the name


object '...' not found
The variable does not exist yet, or R was restarted


$ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
You used $ on a vector, not a data frame


undefined columns selected
A column name is misspelled or wrongly capitalised


argument "x" is missing, with no default
A function was called with no argument


Console shows + not >
R is waiting for you to close a bracket or quote. Press Esc


NA where you expected a number
Missing values. Decide what to do about them, then use na.rm = TRUE

title: Ten Rules for Reading Playtest Data
text:
These ten rules are the spine of this module’s analytics strand. Each one is unpacked in the notes that follow, and every lab will send you back to at least one of them. When a lab says “rule 5 again”, this is the page it means.



Decide what would change your mind before you look at the data. An analysis that cannot come out against you is not an analysis.
A number without a question attached is decoration. Ask the question first, in words, and in the form a designer would ask it.
Know what kind of number you are holding. You cannot average a category, and a 1–5 rating is not a measurement.
Look at the shape before you quote the average. Every summary throws information away; the shape tells you what was thrown.
The mean is the wrong summary more often than you think. Anything skewed — completion times, session lengths, frame times — belongs to the median.
Cleaning is analysis. Every row you drop is a decision with a consequence, and you must be able to say what it was.
Compare distributions, not averages. Two groups with the same mean can be completely different games.
Small samples lie confidently. Report how many people you measured, every time, in the same breath as the result.
Sometimes the rare value is the whole story. Averages hide stutter, crashes, and the one puzzle where everybody quits.
A finding that does not name an action is not finished. What → Pattern → Meaning → Action.
crumbs: Ten Rules for Reading Playtest Data

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
text:
This lab is your first contact with R. You are not expected to have written a line of it before today.
The work is deliberately unglamorous. Before you can find anything interesting in a playtest you have to be able to load the data, look at it, and describe it without making a fool of yourself. That is what this sheet trains.
Everything here uses base R — the functions that ship with the language. You will meet the tidyverse in Lab 02. Learning base R first means you will understand what the tidyverse is doing for you rather than treating it as magic.







Function
What it does




c()
Builds a vector from individual values


length(), class()
How many, and what type


read_csv()
Reads a CSV file into a data frame


str(), head(), nrow(), names()
Look at a data frame without printing all of it


$, [ , ]
Pull out a column, or a slice of rows and columns


mean(), median(), sd(), range()
Describe a numeric variable


quantile(), IQR()
Describe the spread and the tails


table()
Count a categorical variable


hist(), boxplot()
See the shape of a variable

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 01 — Build a vector and look at it [Do]
text:
Exercise 01 — Build a vector and look at it [Do]
Create a vector called deaths holding the death counts from six playtest sessions: 4, 2, 7, 3, 0, 5.
Report how many values it holds and what type R thinks it is.






TipSolution






deaths <- c(4, 2, 7, 3, 0, 5)

deaths

[1] 4 2 7 3 0 5

length(deaths)

[1] 6

class(deaths)

[1] "numeric"


R stores plain numbers as doubles unless you force an integer with 4L.



Write 1 sentence: why does a vector have to hold values of a single type?

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 02 — Pull values out by position [Do]
text:
Exercise 02 — Pull values out by position [Do]
Using deaths from Exercise 01, extract the first value, the third and fifth values, and everything except the first value.






TipSolution






deaths[1]

[1] 4

deaths[c(3, 5)]

[1] 7 0

deaths[-1]

[1] 2 7 3 0 5


Square brackets take a position, a vector of positions, or a negative position meaning “all except this”.



Write 1 sentence: R counts from 1, not 0. If you have written C# or C++, what is the one mistake this will cause you?

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 03 — A missing value poisons the arithmetic [Do]
text:
Exercise 03 — A missing value poisons the arithmetic [Do]
A seventh tester’s death count was not recorded. Add NA to the end of deaths and take the mean. Then take it again so that the result is a number.






TipSolution






deaths <- c(deaths, NA)

mean(deaths)

[1] NA

mean(deaths, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 3.5


NA is not zero and it is not “empty”. It means unknown, and the mean of a set containing an unknown value is itself unknown. R tells you that rather than quietly guessing.



Write 2 sentences: na.rm = TRUE makes the error message go away. Explain why that is not the same thing as fixing the problem.

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 04 — Filter a vector with a condition [Apply]
text:
Exercise 04 — Filter a vector with a condition [Apply]
Using the seven-value deaths vector, produce a TRUE/FALSE vector showing which sessions had more than 3 deaths, use it to extract those death counts, then count how many sessions that is.






TipSolution






deaths > 3

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE    NA

deaths[deaths > 3]

[1]  4  7  5 NA

sum(deaths > 3, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 3


Two things worth noticing. deaths[deaths > 3] keeps the NA, because R does not know whether the unknown value is above 3 or not. And sum() on a TRUE/FALSE vector counts the TRUEs, because TRUE is 1 and FALSE is 0.



Write 1–2 sentences: why is sum(x > 3) a count rather than a total?

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 05 — Build a small table of related vectors [Apply]
text:
Exercise 05 — Build a small table of related vectors [Apply]
Create two more vectors the same length as deaths — player (P01 to P07) and build (alternating "A" and "B", starting with A). Combine all three into a data frame called mini, then show its structure and first three rows.






TipSolution






player <- c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05", "P06", "P07")
build  <- rep(c("A", "B"), length.out = 7)

mini <- data.frame(player, build, deaths)

str(mini)

'data.frame':   7 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ player: chr  "P01" "P02" "P03" "P04" ...
 $ build : chr  "A" "B" "A" "B" ...
 $ deaths: num  4 2 7 3 0 5 NA

head(mini, 3)

  player build deaths
1    P01     A      4
2    P02     B      2
3    P03     A      7


rep() with length.out repeats a pattern until it reaches the length you asked for — useful for generating alternating conditions.



Write 1 sentence: what does a data frame give you that three separate vectors do not?

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 07 — Get at a single column [Do]
text:
Exercise 07 — Get at a single column [Do]
Extract the score column three different ways: with $, with [[ ]], and with [ , ]. Confirm all three give the same thing.






TipSolution






by_dollar  <- sessions$score
by_bracket <- sessions[["score"]]
by_comma   <- sessions[, "score", drop = TRUE]

identical(by_dollar, by_bracket)

[1] TRUE

identical(by_dollar, by_comma)

[1] TRUE


drop = TRUE matters: without it, [ , ] on a tibble hands you back a one-column table rather than a plain vector, and the identical check fails.
Note the variable names. Never call a variable c — you would be shadowing c(), the function you used to build every vector in Part A.



Write 1 sentence: which of the three would you use in a script another person has to read, and why?

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
text:
Exercise 08 — Classify every column [Apply]
For each of these columns, state whether it is nominal, ordinal, discrete or continuous: cohort, archetype, build, score, kills, deaths, session_minutes, quit_reason.






TipSolution













Column
Type
Why




cohort
Ordinal
Novice → Regular → Veteran has a real order


archetype
Nominal
Scout is not more or less than Sentinel


build
Nominal
Two labels, no order


score
Discrete
Whole points, though large enough to treat as continuous


kills
Discrete
A count


deaths
Discrete
A count


session_minutes
Continuous
Measured time, one decimal place


quit_reason
Nominal
Four labels, no order



The interesting one is cohort. R has loaded it as chr — plain text — and will sort it alphabetically as Novice, Regular, Veteran, which happens to be the right order by accident. Never rely on that.



Write 2 sentences: pick one column above and explain what would go wrong if you treated it as the wrong type.

section: Exercise 10 — Describe a numeric variable properly [Apply]
text:
Exercise 10 — Describe a numeric variable properly [Apply]
For score and for session_minutes, compute the mean, median, standard deviation, range, quartiles and IQR.






TipSolution






mean(sessions$score)

[1] 1428.767

median(sessions$score)

[1] 1470

sd(sessions$score)

[1] 319.2236

range(sessions$score)

[1]  541 2019

quantile(sessions$score)

     0%     25%     50%     75%    100% 
 541.00 1270.00 1470.00 1628.75 2019.00 

IQR(sessions$score)

[1] 358.75

summary(sessions$session_minutes)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   7.70   15.50   26.15   22.77   29.32   32.00 

IQR(sessions$session_minutes)

[1] 13.825


summary() gives minimum, quartiles, median, mean and maximum in one call, which is usually where to start. quantile() is there for when you need a specific percentile rather than the standard five.



Write 2 sentences: express the gap between mean and median as a percentage of the median, for both variables. Which one is more skewed, and does its tail run left or right?






NoteCheck your answer





Score sits 2.8% below its median. Session minutes sits 12.9% below. Both are left-skewed — the mean falls below the median because a group of short sessions drags it down — but session minutes is far more so.
Comparing the raw gaps (-41 points against -3.4 minutes) would have told you the opposite, which is why the scale of the variable always has to come into it.

section: Exercise 12 — Split a numeric variable by a group [Apply]
text:
Exercise 12 — Split a numeric variable by a group [Apply]
Draw boxplots of score split by archetype, in one plot.






TipSolution






boxplot(score ~ archetype,
        data = sessions,
        main = "Score by archetype",
        ylab = "Score",
        col  = "grey85")

Write 2 sentences: one archetype has a much larger spread than the others. Which one, and why is “larger spread” a more useful observation here than “lower average”?

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
These are the questions that come up in the week after a playtest. None of them is exotic. All of them are painful to answer with a spreadsheet, and each one is answered below by a single figure and a few dozen lines of R.



The question you are actually asking
Answered by




I have 120 rows of results and no idea what is in them. Where do I start?
View 1


All four characters average about the same score. Does that mean they are balanced?
View 2


I designed four classes to play differently. Did they stay different once real people played them?
View 3


I want players to score higher. Which ability is actually worth buffing?
View 4


Testers keep giving up partway through. When do I lose them, and is it the same moment every time?
View 5


The survey came back with 960 ratings across eight questions. Which complaint do I fix first?
View 6


My frame-rate counter says 60 FPS. My testers say the game stutters. Who is lying?
View 7


How can I find where players are loitering, sniping, or being funnelled into a kill zone?
View 8


Which parts of my level is nobody using?
View 8


How did one particular player move through the level — did they learn the route, or wander?
View 8b



Every one of these is a question about your own game, asked of data your own engine can already record. The only thing missing is the ability to read it.

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
Before you read any code
This document is a showcase, not a lesson. Nothing here is examinable and you are not expected to understand the code yet. Its only job is to show you what six hours of R can do to a pile of raw playtest numbers.
Every figure below was produced from four CSV files, in between eleven and fifty-five lines of code. By the end of these notes you will be able to produce all of them.






NoteThe data



Tidebreak is a fictional four-player top-down arena, used here so that the example is self-contained. The playtest recorded four things:








File
One row per
Holds




tidebreak_sessions.csv
player, per session
Six end-of-match ability ratings, eleven match statistics, session length and quit reason, for 120 sessions


tidebreak_survey.csv
player, per session
Eight agreement items rated 1 to 5


tidebreak_frame_times.csv
rendered frame
Frame time in milliseconds, by build and level zone


tidebreak_positions.csv
player, per second
Top-down position for eight players across one 180-second match



All four are synthetic, but they behave like the real thing: the numbers are messy, the interesting findings are not the obvious ones, and at least two widely held assumptions about the game turn out to be wrong.




Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

sessions    <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv")
survey      <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_survey.csv")
frame_times <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_frame_times.csv")
positions   <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_positions.csv")
level       <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_level.csv")

# A small, fixed palette used by every figure in this document.
pal <- c(blue = "#2a78d6", orange = "#eb6834", aqua = "#1baf7a", yellow = "#eda100")
ink <- c(primary = "#0b0b0b", secondary = "#52514e", grid = "#e6e5e1")

# Each archetype keeps the same colour in every figure, so that a colour always
# means the same thing no matter which chart you are looking at.
arch_pal <- c(Scout = pal[["blue"]],  Sentinel = pal[["orange"]],
              Engineer = pal[["aqua"]], Duelist = pal[["yellow"]])

# Likewise for the two builds, which appear in Views 5 and 7.
build_pal <- c(A = pal[["orange"]], B = pal[["blue"]])

theme_tb <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink["primary"], size = 13),
      plot.subtitle   = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"], size = 11),
      axis.title      = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"], size = 10),
      axis.text       = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"]),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = ink["grid"], linewidth = 0.3),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 1 — The table you can actually read
text:
View 1 — The table you can actually read
Question: what happened in each session?
Before you analyse anything you need to be able to look at your data. A raw CSV in Excel is awkward at 120 rows and unusable at 120,000. A rendered table is searchable and sortable, and it goes straight into a report.
Sort by Score, or type Sentinel into the search box, and you will already see the finding that View 2 makes formal.


Show the code
sessions %>%
  select(Session = session_id, Player = player_id, Cohort = cohort,
         Archetype = archetype, Build = build, Score = score,
         Kills = kills, Deaths = deaths, `Alive (s)` = time_alive_s,
         Awareness = awareness) %>%
  datatable(
    rownames = FALSE,
    options  = list(pageLength = 8, dom = "ftip", scrollX = TRUE),
    caption  = "Tidebreak playtest: 120 sessions"
  ) %>%
  formatStyle("Score",
    background = styleColorBar(range(sessions$score), "#cde2fb"),
    backgroundSize = "98% 60%", backgroundRepeat = "no-repeat",
    backgroundPosition = "center")

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 2 — Distributions, not averages
Question: which archetype performs best?
The tempting answer is to compare four average scores. Do that here and the archetypes look almost identical, which would be a design decision made on a misreading.
A violin plot draws the whole distribution. Read the Sentinel shape: it is not one hump but two. Sentinel runs either anchor the objective and score well, or collapse in the opening seconds and score badly. There is almost no middle. That is a balance problem an average would have hidden completely.


Show the code
sessions %>%
  mutate(archetype = fct_reorder(archetype, score, .fun = median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(archetype, score, fill = archetype)) +
  geom_violin(colour = NA, alpha = 0.85, width = 0.9) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", colour = ink[["secondary"]],
               outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title    = "Sentinel is bimodal: it either anchors the round or dies in it",
    subtitle = "Score distribution by archetype, 30 sessions each. Box shows median and interquartile range.",
    x = NULL, y = "Score"
  ) +
  theme_tb()

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 3 — Six numbers as a shape
text:
View 3 — Six numbers as a shape
Question: are the four archetypes actually playing differently?
Each session ends with six ability ratings on a 0–100 scale. Comparing four archetypes across six measures means twenty-four numbers, which no one can hold in their head. Drawn as a radar, each archetype becomes a shape you can recognise at a glance, and the grey outline behind each one is the all-player average for reference.
The shapes are distinct and they are roughly the shapes the design intended. That is the result you want from this chart: confirmation that the archetypes are not quietly converging on the same playstyle.


Show the code
metrics <- c("accuracy", "mobility", "survivability",
             "objective_control", "support", "awareness")

pretty <- c(accuracy = "Accuracy", mobility = "Mobility",
            survivability = "Survival", objective_control = "Objective",
            support = "Support", awareness = "Awareness")

long <- sessions %>%
  select(archetype, all_of(metrics)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-archetype, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(metric = factor(pretty[metric], levels = unname(pretty)))

by_arch <- long %>% group_by(archetype, metric) %>% summarise(value = mean(value))
overall <- long %>% group_by(metric) %>% summarise(value = mean(value))

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = overall, aes(metric, value, group = 1),
               fill = NA, colour = ink[["grid"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_polygon(data = by_arch,
               aes(metric, value, group = archetype, fill = archetype, colour = archetype),
               alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = by_arch, aes(metric, value, colour = archetype), size = 1.8) +
  coord_polar(clip = "off") +
  facet_wrap(~archetype, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = c(25, 50, 75)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Four archetypes, four distinct ability profiles",
    subtitle = "Mean end-of-match rating per ability. Grey outline is the all-player average.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x   = element_text(size = 7),
        strip.text    = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]),
        panel.spacing = unit(1.6, "lines"),
        plot.margin   = margin(10, 20, 10, 20))

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 4 — What actually drives score
Question: which abilities and behaviours move the scoreboard?
A correlogram puts every pair of variables in one picture. Blue means the two rise together, red means one rises as the other falls, and pale means no relationship at all.
Three things to read off it:

Awareness is the strongest positive correlate of score. Map knowledge beats mechanical skill in this build.
Shots fired is essentially uncorrelated with score. Players who shoot more do not win more, which contradicts what the team assumed.
Mobility and survivability pull against each other, which is the intended trade-off working as designed.



Show the code
vars <- c("accuracy", "mobility", "survivability", "objective_control",
          "support", "awareness", "shots_fired", "distance_m",
          "kills", "deaths", "objectives", "score")

nice <- c(accuracy = "Accuracy", mobility = "Mobility", survivability = "Survival",
          objective_control = "Objective ctrl", support = "Support",
          awareness = "Awareness", shots_fired = "Shots fired",
          distance_m = "Distance", kills = "Kills", deaths = "Deaths",
          objectives = "Objectives", score = "Score")

cm <- cor(sessions[vars])
ord <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cm))$order
lv  <- nice[vars[ord]]

cm_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cm)) %>%
  setNames(c("a", "b", "r")) %>%
  mutate(a = factor(nice[as.character(a)], levels = lv),
         b = factor(nice[as.character(b)], levels = lv)) %>%
  filter(as.integer(a) < as.integer(b))   # lower triangle only; the diagonal is always 1

ggplot(cm_long, aes(a, b, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r),
                colour = abs(r) > 0.55), size = 2.9) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e34948", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#2a78d6",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "r") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = ink[["secondary"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    title    = "Awareness drives score; shots fired does not",
    subtitle = "Pearson correlation between every pair of measures, 120 sessions.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text.x       = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position   = "right",
        panel.grid.major  = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor  = element_blank())

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 5 — When people stop playing
Question: we changed how the game explains its objective. Did it keep anyone?
A retention curve shows what fraction of participants were still playing at each minute of the test. It is the shape that matters, not the endpoint: a smooth decay means people drifted away, a cliff means something specific pushed them out.
Build A has a cliff. Between minutes 11 and 13 it drops from 88% to 68%, and 15 of the 17 people who left in that window are logged as frustration quits. Build B, which explains its objective differently, is still at 90% at minute 13 and loses five people to frustration across the whole test against Build A’s twenty.
Now look at what a summary table would have told you: median session length is 23.2 minutes for Build A and 27.1 for Build B. That reads as a modest improvement. The curve shows something else — one specific, fixable moment where a fifth of the Build A testers gave up.


Show the code
minutes <- seq(0, 32, by = 0.25)

retention <- map_dfr(c("A", "B"), function(b) {
  lengths <- sessions %>% filter(build == b) %>% pull(session_minutes)
  tibble(build = b, minute = minutes,
         pct = map_dbl(minutes, ~ 100 * mean(lengths >= .x)))
})

ends <- retention %>% group_by(build) %>% slice_max(minute, n = 1)

ggplot(retention, aes(minute, pct, colour = build)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 11, xmax = 13, ymin = 0, ymax = 100,
           fill = ink[["grid"]], alpha = 0.55) +
  annotate("text", x = 13.4, y = 24, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "88% to 68% in two minutes,\nalmost all frustration quits") +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.1, direction = "hv") +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = paste0("Build ", build)),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.6, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold",
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = build_pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 37), breaks = seq(0, 30, 5),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, " min")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(y) paste0(y, "%")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Build A loses people at a cliff; Build B does not",
    subtitle = "Percentage of participants still playing, by minute of the test session.",
    x = NULL, y = "Still playing"
  ) +
  theme_tb()

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 6 — What players said, ranked by how badly it went
text:
View 6 — What players said, ranked by how badly it went
Question: the survey has eight questions and 120 responses. Which one should we act on first?
Eight averages tell you almost nothing, because a mean of 3.0 can mean everyone was indifferent or that half loved it and half hated it. A diverging bar chart splits each item at the neutral response: disagreement runs left, agreement runs right, and the items sort by the net.
The result is uncomfortable in the way real survey results usually are. The art is the best-rated thing in the game by a distance. The worst-rated item is whether players ever knew what they were supposed to be doing — the same thing that drives the cliff in View 5. People praise the visuals and quit over the design.


Show the code
item_label <- c(
  objective_clear     = "I always knew what my objective was",
  death_understood    = "I understood why I died",
  difficulty_fair     = "The difficulty felt fair",
  level_navigable     = "The level was easy to navigate",
  would_play_again    = "I would play this again",
  match_length        = "The match length felt right",
  controls_responsive = "The controls felt responsive",
  visual_style        = "The visual style is appealing"
)

resp_label <- c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree")

props <- survey %>%
  pivot_longer(-session_id, names_to = "item", values_to = "resp") %>%
  count(item, resp) %>%
  complete(item, resp = 1:5, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  group_by(item) %>% mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup()

# Net agreement decides the order; the neutral block is split so the bars
# pivot on a true zero rather than on the left edge.
ranking <- props %>%
  group_by(item) %>%
  summarise(net = sum(pct[resp >= 4]) - sum(pct[resp <= 2])) %>%
  arrange(net)

item_levels <- unname(item_label[ranking$item])

as_bars <- function(d, sign) {
  d %>%
    mutate(signed = sign * if_else(resp == 3, pct / 2, pct),
           item   = factor(unname(item_label[item]), levels = item_levels),
           resp   = factor(resp_label[resp], levels = resp_label))
}

# The two sides stack in opposite directions, so that the strongest opinion
# always sits furthest from the centre line.
bars_neg <- props %>% filter(resp <= 3) %>% as_bars(-1)
bars_pos <- props %>% filter(resp >= 3) %>% as_bars(+1)

ranking <- ranking %>%
  mutate(item = factor(unname(item_label[item]), levels = item_levels))

ggplot(mapping = aes(signed, item, fill = resp)) +
  geom_col(data = bars_neg, width = 0.72, position = position_stack()) +
  geom_col(data = bars_pos, width = 0.72, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#fcfcfb", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = ranking, aes(x = 106, y = item, label = sprintf("%+.0f", net)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.3, fontface = "bold",
            colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Strongly disagree" = "#e34948",
                               "Disagree"          = "#f2a9a8",
                               "Neutral"           = "#d9d8d4",
                               "Agree"             = "#9ec5f4",
                               "Strongly agree"    = "#2a78d6")) +
  # coord_cartesian zooms; scale limits would DROP the segments that fall
  # outside them, silently truncating the longest bars.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-60, 90, 30),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "%")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-68, 112)) +
  labs(
    title    = "They love the art and cannot tell what the game wants",
    subtitle = "Share of 120 responses. Bars pivot on neutral; the number is net agreement.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.text     = element_text(size = 9),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 7 — The frame-rate counter is lying to you
text:
View 7 — The frame-rate counter is lying to you
Question: both builds average about 59 FPS. Testers say Build B stutters. Who is right?
Both are. Average frame rate is a mean, and a mean is exactly the wrong summary for a quantity where the rare bad values are the entire user experience. Build B renders almost every frame slightly faster than Build A. It also renders one frame in every twenty-five — about twice a second — in 35 to 55 ms instead of 17, and only in one zone of the level: the corridor that View 8 identifies as the choke point.
The trace shows it. The table shows why the FPS readout missed it: the two builds are separated by 0.05 ms at the mean and by 20 ms at the 99th percentile.


Show the code
ggplot(frame_times %>% filter(zone == "Corridor", frame <= 400),
       aes(frame, ms, colour = build)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1000 / 60, linetype = "22",
             colour = ink[["secondary"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~build, ncol = 1, labeller = labeller(build = function(b) paste("Build", b))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = build_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60), breaks = c(1000/60, 30, 45, 60),
                     labels = c("16.7\n(60 FPS)", "30", "45", "60")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Identical average, one of them unplayable",
    subtitle = "Frame time in the Corridor zone, first 400 frames. Dashed line is the 60 FPS budget.",
    x = "Frame", y = "Frame time (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]))











Show the code
frame_times %>%
  group_by(Build = build) %>%
  summarise(
    `Mean FPS`     = round(1000 / mean(ms), 1),
    `Mean (ms)`    = round(mean(ms), 2),
    `Median (ms)`  = round(median(ms), 1),
    `95th (ms)`    = round(quantile(ms, 0.95), 1),
    `99th (ms)`    = round(quantile(ms, 0.99), 1),
    `Worst (ms)`   = round(max(ms), 1)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Every column agrees the builds are the same until the last two.")

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 8 — Where players actually stand
Question: where are the choke points, the camping spots and the dead space?
This is the figure that changes level layouts. The blue field is total time spent per square metre across the whole match. The moving dots are the eight players, one frame per second, coloured by whether they are moving, loitering or holding position. Dark blocks are cover; the block in the north-east is the raised gantry.
Press play, or drag the slider.
Three readings, all of them actionable:

The gap between the central core and the east block carries almost all lateral traffic, and 14 of the 20 deaths in this match happened inside it. That is a choke point.
Two players spend the entire match holding the north-east gantry. Long dwell, no movement, high kill share: a sniper perch.
The west corner is never visited by anyone. That is floor space the level is paying for and not using.



Show the code
# Time spent per 2m x 2m cell, for the background field.
gx_seq <- seq(1, 59, 2)
gy_seq <- seq(1, 39, 2)

field <- positions %>%
  mutate(gx = floor(x / 2) * 2 + 1, gy = floor(y / 2) * 2 + 1) %>%
  count(gx, gy) %>%
  complete(gx = gx_seq, gy = gy_seq, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  arrange(gy, gx)

z <- matrix(field$n, nrow = length(gy_seq), ncol = length(gx_seq), byrow = TRUE)

# Level geometry drawn as rectangles behind the data.
shapes <- pmap(level, function(block, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, kind) {
  list(type = "rect", x0 = xmin, x1 = xmax, y0 = ymin, y1 = ymax,
       fillcolor = if (kind == "elevated") "#6f6e6a" else "#2f2e2c",
       # The gantry is walkable, so it stays translucent and the dwell field
       # underneath it still reads.
       opacity = if (kind == "elevated") 0.35 else 0.92,
       line = list(width = 0), layer = "above")
})

# The animated layer starts at the first second where all three states occur, so
# that the legend is complete from the first frame.
first_full <- positions %>%
  group_by(t) %>% summarise(k = n_distinct(state)) %>%
  filter(k == 3) %>% slice_min(t) %>% pull(t)

deaths <- positions %>% filter(event == "death")

plot_ly(height = 560) %>%
  add_heatmap(
    x = gx_seq, y = gy_seq, z = z, zmin = 0, zmax = 60,
    colorscale = list(c(0, "#fcfcfb"), c(0.25, "#cde2fb"),
                      c(0.6, "#5598e7"), c(1, "#104281")),
    showscale = TRUE, hoverinfo = "z",
    colorbar = list(title = "Seconds\nspent", len = 0.55, thickness = 12,
                    y = 0.72, ticksuffix = "  ")
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = deaths, x = ~x, y = ~y, name = "Death",
    marker = list(symbol = "x", size = 11, color = "#e34948",
                  line = list(color = "#fcfcfb", width = 1)),
    text = ~paste0("death · ", player_id, " · t=", t, "s"), hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = positions %>% filter(t >= first_full),
    x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~t, color = ~state,
    colors = c(Holding = pal[["orange"]], Loitering = pal[["aqua"]],
               Moving = pal[["blue"]]),
    marker = list(size = 13, line = list(color = "#fcfcfb", width = 2)),
    text = ~paste0(player_id, " · t=", t, "s · ", state),
    hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title  = list(text = "<b>One corridor carries the traffic and most of the deaths</b>",
                  x = 0, font = list(size = 14)),
    shapes = shapes,
    xaxis  = list(title = "x (m)", range = c(0, 60), constrain = "domain"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "y (m)", range = c(0, 40), scaleanchor = "x"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, title = list(text = "")),
    margin = list(t = 80)
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 90, transition = 45, redraw = FALSE) %>%
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "t = ", suffix = " s"))







Following one player
The map above answers questions about the level. To ask questions about a player — did they learn the route, did they loop, did they ever leave their corner — you need to follow one of them.
First, all eight routes at once. The line darkens as the match progresses, so you can read direction without playing anything. P03 covers the most ground (268 m). P07 travels almost as far (190 m) without ever leaving a two-metre-wide lane — it shuttles up and down the same corridor for the whole match. P01 and P02 manage 51 m and 35 m between them across three minutes.


Show the code
walls <- level %>% filter(kind != "elevated")
raised <- level %>% filter(kind == "elevated")

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = walls, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
            fill = "#2f2e2c", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_rect(data = raised, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
            fill = "#6f6e6a", alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_path(data = positions, aes(x, y, colour = t), linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~player_id, nrow = 2) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#cde2fb", high = "#104281",
                        name = "Time (s)", breaks = c(1, 90, 180)) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, 60), ylim = c(0, 40), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Eight routes through the same three minutes",
    subtitle = "Line darkens as the match progresses. Two players never leave the gantry.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text         = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major  = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor  = element_blank(),
        strip.text        = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]),
        legend.position   = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(0.9, "lines"))









Now one player, animated, with the trail drawn behind them. Change focus_player to any ID from the panel above and re-run the chunk. The orange dots mark every second this player spent holding position, so you can see where they will stop before they get there.


Show the code
focus_player <- "P06"

path <- positions %>% filter(player_id == focus_player) %>% arrange(t)

# For each second, every position up to that second: this is what makes the
# trail grow rather than jump.
trail <- map_dfr(path$t, function(k) path %>% filter(t <= k) %>% mutate(f = k))

plot_ly(height = 560) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = path %>% filter(state == "Holding"), x = ~x, y = ~y,
    name = "Held position",
    marker = list(size = 7, color = pal[["orange"]], opacity = 0.7),
    text = ~paste0("holding · t=", t, "s"), hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = path %>% slice(1), x = ~x, y = ~y, name = "Start",
    marker = list(symbol = "circle-open", size = 16, color = ink[["primary"]],
                  line = list(width = 2.5)),
    hoverinfo = "text", text = "start"
  ) %>%
  add_paths(
    data = trail, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~f,
    line = list(color = pal[["blue"]], width = 2.5),
    opacity = 0.8, showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = "skip"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = path, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~t,
    marker = list(size = 16, color = pal[["blue"]],
                  line = list(color = "#fcfcfb", width = 2.5)),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    text = ~paste0(focus_player, " · t=", t, "s · ", state), hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title  = list(text = paste0("<b>", focus_player, "'s route through the match</b>"),
                  x = 0, font = list(size = 14)),
    shapes = shapes,
    xaxis  = list(title = "x (m)", range = c(0, 60), constrain = "domain"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "y (m)", range = c(0, 40), scaleanchor = "x"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, title = list(text = "")),
    margin = list(t = 80)
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 70, transition = 0, redraw = FALSE) %>%
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "t = ", suffix = " s"))

None of this is difficult, and most of the length in Views 3 onwards is labelling and styling rather than analysis. All of it is repeatable: the same code runs unchanged on next week’s build, which is the real reason to write analysis as code rather than clicking through a spreadsheet.
The rest of these notes teach you the parts, in order, starting with the question that matters most: what are you actually trying to find out?

title: Describing What You Have
text: Before comparing anything to anything, you have to be able to say what a single variable looks like. This section is the vocabulary for that, and it is the part students most often skip and most often get caught by.

title: Describing What You Have
section: What Kind of Number Is This?
text:
What Kind of Number Is This?
Four types, and the type decides which operations are legal.
Nominal — labels with no order. Character class, platform, quit reason. You can count them. You cannot average them. The mean of Scout and Sentinel does not exist, and if your code produces one, something has gone wrong upstream.
Ordinal — ordered labels with unknown gaps. Difficulty setting, player experience level, and every agreement scale ever printed. Novice, Regular and Veteran are in an order, but Regular is not “halfway” between the other two in any meaningful sense.
Discrete — counts. Deaths, kills, items collected. Whole numbers, and there is no such thing as 2.4 deaths in a single session — though the average number of deaths across many sessions is perfectly meaningful at 2.4.
Continuous — measurements. Completion time, frame time, distance travelled. Any value in a range, limited only by the precision of your instrument.
The awkward case is the rating scale, and it is awkward every time. A 1–5 agreement scale is strictly ordinal: you know Agree is above Neutral, but you do not know that the step from Disagree to Neutral is the same size as the step from Agree to Strongly Agree. In practice, when a scale has five or more points and the responses are reasonably spread, people treat it as numeric and average it. That convention is defensible and universal, and you should still know you are making an assumption. Where it matters — where the whole finding rests on a mean of 3.2 against 3.4 — report the distribution instead.

title: Describing What You Have
section: Tidy Data: One Row Per Observation
text:
Tidy Data: One Row Per Observation
Data arrives in whatever shape the tool that produced it happened to use. Almost all analysis assumes one particular shape, and it is worth naming.
A table is tidy when each row is one observation, each column is one variable, and each cell is one value. For a playtest: one row per player per session, one column per thing you recorded.
The most common violation is a survey export, where the eight questions become eight columns. That is convenient to read and inconvenient to analyse, because “question” is really a variable and its eight values have been spread across the column headings. Reshaping it into one row per player per question is what makes the whole survey analysable in one operation, and you will do exactly that in Lab 03.

title: Describing What You Have
text:
Centre
Two summaries of “the typical value”, and choosing between them is a real decision, not a formality.
The mean adds everything and divides by the count. It uses every value, which is its strength, and it is dragged by extremes, which is its weakness.
The median is the middle value when sorted. Half above, half below. It ignores how extreme the extremes are, which is its strength and its weakness.
When they disagree, the data is skewed, and the gap tells you which way. If the mean sits well above the median, a few large values are pulling it up: a long right tail. If it sits below, a group of small values is pulling it down.
For game data this is not an edge case, it is the norm. Completion times, session lengths and frame times are all skewed almost by construction — there is a floor on how fast anyone can finish and no ceiling on how slow. Default to the median for anything time-like and reach for the mean only when you have looked at the shape and satisfied yourself it is roughly symmetric.
When you compare the two, compare them relative to the size of the variable. A gap of 40 points on a score in the thousands is nothing; a gap of 3 minutes on a median of 26 is a real skew.

title: Describing What You Have
text:
Spread
The centre alone is nearly useless. Two levels with identical average completion times, one where everybody takes four minutes and one where half take one minute and half take seven, are not the same level.
Range is minimum to maximum. Easy to quote and almost always misleading, since a single unusual value defines it entirely.
Standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean. It is the right measure for roughly symmetric data and it inherits the mean’s sensitivity to extremes.
Quartiles split the sorted data into four. The first quartile has a quarter below it, the third has three quarters. The interquartile range — the distance between them — is the width of the middle half of your players, and it is the most robust description of spread you have. For skewed game data, quote the median and the IQR together.
Percentiles generalise this: the 95th percentile has 95% of values below it. Sections 5 will show you why the 99th percentile of frame time is the single most important number in a performance capture.

title: Describing What You Have
text:
Look at the Shape First
Every summary statistic throws information away. That is what a summary is for. The risk is that it throws away the finding.
A histogram shows you the whole distribution: where the bulk sits, whether it is symmetric, whether there is a second hump, whether there are outliers. Draw one before quoting any average. It costs one line.
The number of bins changes what you see, sometimes dramatically. Too few and a second hump disappears; too many and noise looks like structure. Try several. That a chart changes with its settings is not a flaw to hide — it is the first evidence that a chart is an argument rather than a fact, and you are responsible for the argument you make.
A boxplot compresses the same information into median, quartiles and outliers. It is less informative than a histogram for one variable and much better for comparing several groups side by side, which is what Section 4 is about.
Two humps are always worth chasing. A distribution with two peaks usually means two populations have been mixed: players who found the key and players who did not, sessions that completed and sessions that crashed. The average of a bimodal distribution describes nobody at all — it names a value that sits in the valley between the two groups, where the fewest players actually are.

title: Describing What You Have
text:
Reflective Questions

Take a variable from your own project’s telemetry. Which of the four types is it, and what would break if you treated it as the type next door?
Why is the median usually the right summary for completion time, but not for something like accuracy percentage?
You draw a histogram of level completion times and see two clear humps. List three things that could have caused that, and say how you would tell them apart.
A teammate reports “average session length is 22 minutes”. What two further numbers would you ask for before letting that into a report?

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Every team makes decisions about their game constantly. Most of those decisions are made from memory, taste and the loudest voice in the room, and most of the time that is fine — taste is why anyone plays your game rather than a spreadsheet.
Measurement earns its place in the cases where taste reliably fails. There are three of them, and they recur in every project.
You cannot see your own game any more. You have played your level five hundred times. You know where the key is. You cannot un-know it, and no amount of care will let you experience your own tutorial as a stranger. This is the single most common cause of a game that the team finds obvious and the player finds impenetrable.
You cannot feel a rare event. A stutter that happens once every two seconds occupies less than one per cent of frames. Your average frame rate will not show it. Your players will talk about nothing else.
You cannot remember twenty playtests. After a session you remember the two people who struggled most and the last person you watched. You do not remember the distribution, and you will confidently reconstruct one that never existed.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
The Three Sources
Almost everything you will analyse in a game project comes from one of three places, and they have very different characters.
Telemetry is what the game records about itself while it runs: positions, events, deaths, times, item pickups. It is objective, it arrives in enormous quantities, and it tells you what happened and never why. Telemetry is cheap to collect and easy to collect badly — a log with no session identifier or no timestamp is close to worthless.
Performance capture is a special case of telemetry with its own conventions and its own failure modes. Frame times, memory, draw calls. It is the one area where the standard summary — average frame rate — is actively misleading, which is why Section 5 spends its time there.
Asking people is surveys, interviews and think-aloud sessions. It is the only source that tells you why, and the least reliable. People misremember, they are polite, they rationalise, and they answer the question they think you meant. A survey tells you what a player believes about their experience, which is a real and useful thing, but it is not the same as what happened.
The three disagree, and that is the point. The most valuable finding in any playtest is usually the place where telemetry and opinion contradict each other: players say the level is fine and the heat map shows nobody finds the side route; players say the game runs smoothly and the frame log shows a hitch every two seconds. A team with only one source never finds these.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
section: Turning a Vague Question into a Measurable One
text:
Turning a Vague Question into a Measurable One
The question a designer asks is almost never answerable as asked.







What you are asked
What you can actually measure




“Is the level too hard?”
Deaths per attempt; time to first completion; proportion who never finish; where attempts end


“Does the game feel good?”
Time to first successful interaction; retry rate after failure; rated responsiveness


“Is the tutorial working?”
Proportion who use the taught mechanic later, unprompted


“Do people like the art?”
Rated appeal; which screenshots they choose; where they stop to look



Notice that each right-hand cell names a specific number you could write down after watching one person play. That is the test. If you cannot describe how you would record it for a single player, you have not finished turning the question into a measurement.
Notice also that the right-hand column is often not one measure but several, and that they can disagree. This is not a failure of the method. A tutorial that everybody completes and nobody learns from is a real and common outcome, and only two measures together can find it.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Deciding in Advance
Before you collect anything, write down what result would change your mind. “If more than a third of testers never find the second key, I will add a light cue.”
This costs nothing and protects you from the most comfortable mistake in the discipline: running the test, getting an ambiguous result, and finding in it whatever you already believed. If the threshold is written down beforehand, the data gets to answer. If it is not, you will answer and attribute it to the data.

title: Why Developers Measure Anything
text:
Reflective Questions

Pick a mechanic in your own project. Write the designer’s question, then three different measures that would bear on it, then say which one you would trust most and why.
Name something about your own game that you can no longer judge, because you have played it too often.
Your team disagrees about whether a puzzle is too obscure. What number, recorded from a single playtester, would settle it?
